draft.title: Ecosystem services
card: Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from ecosystems. People often receive them without paying for them.
Some services supply things we use, such as food, timber and fresh water. Others regulate natural processes, such as wetlands soaking up floodwater or insects pollinating crops.
Ecosystems also give cultural value. A river, forest or reef can be a place for recreation, learning, beauty or spiritual connection.
When an ecosystem is damaged, the services it gives can be reduced. People may then have to replace them, for example by building a water treatment plant.
draft.remember: Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from nature, from food and clean water to flood protection and cultural value.

a.q: Which of these is an ecosystem service?
opts: Mangroves absorbing wave energy and protecting a town
A council building a concrete sea wall to protect a town
A farmer buying honey bees to pollinate an orchard
A company bottling and selling tap water to shoppers
a.why: Mangroves are part of an ecosystem, and they give a benefit to people by protecting the town from waves. The sea wall, hired bees and bottled water are human-made substitutes, so they are not services from an ecosystem.
a.clue: Look for a benefit that comes from nature itself.

b.q: Wetlands near Wagga Wagga are drained for farmland. Later, a flood damages nearby homes more than past floods did. Which ecosystem service was most likely lost?
opts: Flood protection from the wetlands soaking up water
Food supply from the wetlands feeding local people
Pollination of crops by insects living in the wetlands
Cultural value of the wetlands as a place to visit
b.why: Wetlands can soak up floodwater, so draining them can make floods worse for nearby homes. Food, pollination and cultural value may also change, but the extra flood damage points to the loss of flood protection.
b.clue: Which service links to what happened during the flood?

a.best: Mangroves absorbing wave energy and protecting a town

b.best: Flood protection from the wetlands soaking up water

problems.detail: The why calls the hired honey bees a 'human-made substitute'. Bees are living animals, not human-made, and pollination by bees is the card's own example of a service. The why should say that buying managed bees is a paid human input that replaces wild pollination, not that the bees are human-made.

The stem is about a flood, and the right option is the only one that mentions floods ('Flood protection'). A student can match the word without understanding ecosystem services, and the clue points to the same match.

proposal.title: Ecosystem services
card: Ecosystem services are the benefits people get from ecosystems. People often receive them without paying for them.
Some services supply things we use, such as food, timber and fresh water. Others regulate natural processes, such as wetlands soaking up floodwater or wild insects pollinating crops.

proposal.remember: Nature supplies goods, regulates processes and gives cultural value, often for free, and damage can leave people paying to replace it.

a.q: Which of these is an ecosystem service?
opts: Mangroves absorbing wave energy and protecting a town
A council building a concrete sea wall to protect a town
A farmer buying honey bees to pollinate an orchard
A company bottling and selling tap water to shoppers
a.why: Mangroves are part of an ecosystem, and they protect the town from waves without anyone paying for it. The sea wall is built by people. Buying managed bees is a paid human input that replaces wild pollination, and bottled water is a product a business sells.
a.clue: Look for a benefit nature gives without anyone paying for it.

b.q: Wetlands near Wagga Wagga are drained for farmland. Later, a flood damages nearby homes more than past floods did. Which service was most likely lost?
opts: Holding rainwater and slowing how fast it runs off
Supplying fish and reeds that people harvest for use
Providing homes for insects that pollinate farm crops
Offering a place for birdwatching and outdoor learning
b.why: Wetlands regulate water by soaking it up and slowing its flow, so draining them can make floods worse for nearby homes. Pollination is also a regulating service, which makes it tempting, but losing it affects crops, not flood damage.
b.clue: Think about what a wetland does with water during heavy rain.
